    Step 1 — Login and progress saving

    Add a login and signup system to the site. Users should be able to create an account with a username and password. Once logged in, save their quiz scores, flashcard progress and minigame high scores to their profile. Show a small profile icon in the top right corner when logged in. Use a database to persist this data between sessions.

    Step 2 — Character and coin system

    Add a character system. When a user creates an account they get a basic avatar shown on their profile page. Add a coin currency called Byte Coins. Users earn Byte Coins by completing quizzes (10 coins per correct answer), finishing minigames (50 coins for completion, bonus for high scores) and flipping all flashcards in a set (25 coins). Show the coin balance in the top navigation bar next to the profile icon.

    Step 3 — Gacha system

    Add a Gacha shop page. Players spend Byte Coins to open loot boxes that contain accessories for their character. Each pull costs 100 Byte Coins. Accessories have four rarity tiers: Common (60% chance), Rare (25% chance), Epic (12% chance) and Legendary (3% chance). Examples of accessories include hats, glasses, backgrounds and outfits themed around computer science (e.g. a circuit board hat, pixel sunglasses, a hoodie with binary code). Show an animated reveal when an accessory is pulled. Players can equip accessories to their character from their profile page. Show a collection screen of all accessories the player owns.

    Step 4 — In-topic balancing scale game

    In each of the four topic sections (Ethical, Legal, Cultural/Social, Environmental) add a mini balancing scale game. Show a set of argument cards relevant to that topic. The player drags argument cards onto either the left side (For / Positive) or right side (Against / Negative) of a set of scales. The scales visually tilt based on how many cards are on each side. When all cards are correctly placed the scales balance and the player earns 30 Byte Coins. If a card is placed on the wrong side it bounces back with a short explanation of why it belongs on the other side.

    Make the following changes to the site all at once: MASTERY BAR OVERHAUL: Replace the current mastery bar system with a tiered XP rank system for each topic. Tiers are Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum and Diamond. XP is earned based on quiz performance not just completion. Scoring full marks awards maximum XP, scoring below 50% awards minimal XP, and scoring zero on written questions awards no XP from those questions. Getting 2 out of 9 correct should fill the bar by no more than 5% not 44%. Written questions must be worth significantly more XP than multiple choice when answered correctly. The mastery bar and current tier should only appear after completing a quiz, styled like Seneca's post-quiz strength indicator, showing XP gained, total XP in current tier and progress to the next tier. Reaching each tier milestone awards a unique topic-specific cosmetic accessory. Diamond tier in any topic awards an ultra-rare cosmetic. The gap in XP required between tiers must increase exponentially so Bronze to Silver is achievable quickly but Gold to Diamond requires consistent high scores across many attempts. Reduce the number of multiple choice questions significantly across all quizzes and replace them with written short answer and keyword matching questions that test genuine recall. Multiple choice should only be used for genuinely tricky concept distinctions not common sense answers. QUIZ ME BUTTON: Remove all inline quizzes from beneath the topic content pages. Replace each one with a single Quiz Me button at the bottom of the topic page. Clicking it opens the quiz as a modal or separate view so the content page stays clean. Each quiz must contain a mix of multiple choice and written short answer questions where the player types a response checked against key terms or marked correct if it contains the right keywords. The mastery bar fills incrementally as the player completes quiz questions over time and persists between sessions so returning to do more questions continues filling the bar from where it left off. COIN BALANCING: Quizzes award 30 coins per correct answer. Minigames award 10 coins per correct answer. Written questions in quizzes award 40 coins per correct answer. This balance should be consistent across the entire site to encourage players to prioritise actual revision over minigames. THEMED TOPIC GAMES: Add a unique themed minigame inside each topic section. Each game must have UI, colours and animations matching its theme. For Ethical Issues keep the balancing scale game but restyle it with a marble and gold philosophy aesthetic. For Legal Issues add a courtroom drama game where the player acts as a judge reading a crime scenario and must select which law was broken from CMA 1990, DPA 2018, CDPA 1988 and FOIA 2000 by choosing from evidence cards laid out on a wooden courtroom desk, with a courtroom background and a gavel animation on correct answers. For Cultural and Social add a city builder style game where the player is shown statements about social and cultural impacts and must drag them into the correct building such as a school for education impacts, a hospital for health and wellbeing impacts and a tower block for digital divide impacts, with an animated city skyline background. For Environmental add a forest survival game where the player answers environmental impact questions and correct answers make an animated tree grow and bloom while wrong answers cause leaves to fall and the tree to wilt, with a nature background and ambient animations. All four games must award coins consistent with the existing coin system at 10 coins per correct answer.     Base44
    Read Auth Context
    Searched bugs

    The root cause is clear: gameContext.jsx does its own base44.auth.me() call independently of AuthContext. In the published version, this races/fails for non-builder users, so data only lives in localStorage. The fix is to make GameProvider use useAuth() directly since it's already inside AuthProvider.

    Edited game Context

    The fix routes all auth through AuthContext instead of gameContext making its own independent base44.auth.me() call. Now GameProvider uses useAuth() to get the authenticated user — the same session that AuthContext already validated. When a user is logged in on the published site, their UserGameState record loads from the database correctly, and all writes sync back to it. The loadedForRef guard prevents re-fetching if the user email hasn't changed.
